context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, postmarked 1 December 1898, Paris. Correcting the proofs of The Importance of Being Earnest for Smithers's edition, published the following February - the last book Wilde saw through the press.
quote:
Taverne F. Pousset, Paris

My dear Smithers, I return the proofs. Will you kindly see if Chasuble is called ‘Chasuble’ or ‘Doctor Chasuble’ in Act II? If he is called ‘Doctor Chasuble’ of course the title, in the headline, should be continued. Shannon will do the cover.

If you don’t hear from Alexander, kindly ask one of your clerks to look up the _Era_ for February — 1895 — about the 14th — all the cast will be there — The Era newspaper, of course: also the _date_ of the production must be given.

Shannon will send you the design in a few days — and of course you will have the same lovely cloth.

The original title was

‘The Importance of being Earnest: a trivial comedy for serious people.’

Will this be too much for the title page? I think not. You must add ‘by the author of Lady Windermere’s Fan’.

Paris is quite wintry: I have not returned to the Moulin Rouge. I hear Miss D’Or has no grandson.

Ever yours Oscar Wilde
original_provenance: Read at HRC 2568, images 54-55 - squared Taverne F. Pousset paper, the blind stamp showing through on side 2: image 54 gives sides 1 and 4, image 55 the inner opening, sides 2 and 3. Emphasis: '_date_' on side 2 is underlined - short, flat, word-width, confirmed at 4.5x - and the volume italicises it. Seventh confirmed case of a printed italic on an ordinary English word recording a real mark. Not a double underline, settled: '_Era_' carries one underline. I read a second stroke below it and proposed a doubling; Lovelle ruled it single, and the lower stroke is the dash of 'February - 1895 -' on the next line, which falls directly beneath the word. That is a new way for this hand to fake a mark, and a mean one, because his dashes are long and his lines are widely spaced: a dash on the following line sits exactly where a second underline would. And the same word again, unmarked: the second 'Era', four lines later in 'The Era newspaper, of course', carries no underline at all. The volume italicises both occurrences identically. So within a single sentence he marks the title once and not the second time, and the edition flattens the difference. Titles: 'Chasuble', 'Doctor Chasuble', the play's full title and 'Lady Windermere's Fan' are all in his inverted commas, not underlined; the volume converts every one to italic, and sets the play title as a centred display. Punctuation: his dashes restored.
